newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan rivals in artillery duel amid peace bid.
newsitem.headline: Afghan rivals in artillery duel amid peace bid.

text.p: Taleban and opposition forces fought a fierce artillery duel north of the Afghan capital Kabul on Saturday as an emissary from neighbouring Pakistan held talks with Taleban officials to discuss peace plans.

The opposition alliance based in the northern town of Mazar-i-Sharif said its forces had advanced several km (miles) closer to Kabul after capturing two small hills overlooking the city, and repeated its demand that the Taleban withdraw from the capital to head off an attack.
There was no independent confirmation of the opposition report of advance. But witnesses in the area reported earlier on Saturday that there was no change in the front line there.

A senior Pakistan Foreign Ministry official, Iftikhar Murshed, held talks with Taleban officials in the southern town of Kandahar to pursue his efforts to arrange intra-Afghan peace talks, Pakistan's state television said.

It said his talks with Taleban Foreign Minister Mullah Abdul Jalil and former foreign minister Mullah Mohammad Ghous centred on forming a political commission to take care of issues such as a ceasefire, exchange of political prisoners and a future broad-based government.

Opposition officials in Mazar-i-Sharif said they did not expect special U.N. envoy Norbert Holl to come there until late next week. He was twice forced to postpone visits this week because top alliance officials were away at front lines.

On Saturday morning, an opposition jet dropped at least one bomb on Taleban positions around Hussein Kot village, some 12 miles (19 km) north of Kabul, while Taleban gunners pounded opposition fighters holding a salient running south to within 13 miles (21 km) of the city, witnesses said.
A Reuters correspondent saw two jets, each with a 200-pound bomb slung under them, take off from Mazar-i-Sharif airport on Saturday and head in the direction of Kabul.

The front lines have remained relatively stable since an advance by the anti-Taleban alliance two weeks ago. The Taleban has retaken some high ground overlooking opposition positions, but there have been no major movements.
Reports from Mazar-i-Sharif, the opposition headquarters, indicated that more than 1,000 opposition fighters have moved towards Kabul in preparation for an attack on the city.

Mohammad Yunus Qanooni, opposition interior minister and chief negotiator with U.N. envoys, said on Saturday the only way to head off an attack on Kabul was for Taleban forces to withdraw completely from there so they were 30 or 40 km (18 or 25 miles) away out of artillery range of the city.
Asked if unarmed Taleban officials could remain in Kabul, Qanooni told Reuters in Mazar-i-Sharif: "There are no unarmed Taleban. They all must go."
"Taleban counter-attacks are getting weaker," Qanooni said.
